title: Compute a CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE Checksum
statement:
A checksum that only catches the mistakes you already expected is not worth
much. CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE is the checksum underneath a lot of embedded
protocols precisely because it does not have that problem -- it is built
from a well-studied polynomial rather than an ad-hoc XOR fold, and it is
merciless about the two things that make CRCs slippery to reimplement:
**bit order** and **initial value**.

This exercise asks for exactly the CCITT-FALSE variant, not "a CRC-16" --
several different, mutually incompatible checksums share the CRC-16/CCITT
name (CCITT-FALSE, XMODEM, MCRF4XX, X-25...), and they differ only in
details that never show up in the polynomial: what the register starts at,
and which end of each byte goes in first. Get either one wrong and you have
implemented a real CRC-16 -- just not this one, and every check value will
be off in a way that looks like a bug in something else.

## Your function

```
uint16_t crc16_ccitt_false(const uint8_t *data, size_t length);
```

Process `data[0..length-1]` **most-significant-bit first**, against
polynomial `0x1021`, with the 16-bit CRC register starting at `0xFFFF`. There
is no final XOR and no bit reflection anywhere in this variant -- the
register you end up with is the answer.

The standard byte-at-a-time form: XOR the next byte into the top eight bits
of the register, then shift the whole 16-bit register left one bit at a time,
eight times, XORing in the polynomial whenever the bit shifted out of the top
was a 1.

## The reference check value

The CRC catalogue's way of confirming an implementation is a fixed input
everyone can try: the nine ASCII bytes `"123456789"` must produce `0x29B1`
under CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE. If your function disagrees with that on this input,
it disagrees with the standard, whatever else it does right.

## Watch out

- **The initial value is `0xFFFF`, not `0x0000`.** Starting from zero is not
  a small deviation -- it is a different, real checksum (CRC-16/XMODEM,
  same polynomial, different init) that happens to only agree with
  CCITT-FALSE on inputs that never make the top bit of the register matter
  before the first byte is folded in. `crc16_ccitt_false` on an **empty**
  buffer is the cleanest place this shows: the correct answer is `0xFFFF`
  itself, since no byte was ever XORed in to change the register from its
  starting value -- an implementation that started from `0` returns `0`
  instead, and a fixed test checks exactly that.
- **This variant is not bit-reflected.** Some CRC-16 variants (MODBUS, ARC)
  process each byte least-significant-bit first and shift the register the
  other way; mixing that convention into a CCITT-FALSE implementation
  produces a plausible-looking 16-bit number that will not match the
  standard check value, or anyone else's implementation of this variant.
  MSB-first, shifting left, is the whole of this variant's bit order.
- `data[i] << 8` promotes `data[i]` to `int` before the shift -- harmless
  here because the result fits comfortably in an `int`, but it is exactly
  the kind of implicit promotion MISRA's essential type model wants a
  reviewer to notice and check, rather than have it pass unremarked.
- A single byte with the top bit set (`0x80`) is worth testing on its own:
  it is the first byte value where a signed-`char` build (if you ever port
  this without `uint8_t`) sign-extends to a negative `int`, and `<< 8` on
  a negative operand is undefined behaviour rather than merely surprising.

tests.name: the standard check value: ASCII "123456789"
tests.description: The CRC catalogue's reference vector for this exact variant -- if this does not match, the bit order or the initial value is wrong.

tests.name: an empty buffer returns the initial value unchanged
tests.description: No byte is ever folded in, so the register never moves from 0xFFFF. A wrong initial value of 0x0000 (CRC-16/XMODEM) returns 0000 here instead.

tests.name: single bytes, including one with the top bit set
tests.description: 0x80 is the first byte value where a signed-char build would sign-extend before the shift; uint8_t sidesteps that entirely.

tests.name: a short buffer with mixed bytes
a leading zero byte is not the same as a shorter buffer
tests.description: Prepending 0x00 changes the checksum -- the byte is processed, not skipped, so the two buffers must not produce the same CRC.
